beats.narration_text: First, the lineup. Claude ships in tiers: Haiku is fast and cheap. Sonnet is the solid middle. Opus is the big one. Then there's a separate naming track for the absolute top model — instead of a number, they give it a name. The current name is Fable-5. It's the smartest AI model by benchmark, better than everything else on reasoning, coding, and long document work. And it has a timeline problem: it launched in June included in paid plans, got briefly banned by the US government on June 12th, came back July 1st at fifty percent of weekly limits, and left subscriptions entirely on July 12th. From that point, Fable runs on usage billing.

A useful framing is the clearest way to think about this. Fable-5 is a senior lawyer with twenty years of experience — one thousand dollars an hour. Sonnet-5 is the capable intern at one hundred an hour. You don't pay the senior partner to review every quick contract. You pay them to define the international strategy, then hand the drafting to the intern. The intern can still read what the senior wrote and execute it well. The disaster scenario: a team of a hundred people, nobody trained on which model to use, everyone defaults to Fable for everything. The failure scenario: a million-dollar Anthropic invoice. Not fun.

The key insight: don't prompt Fable-5. That sounds counterintuitive, but here's what it means. The old habit — typing a long, detailed prompt into the top model — is not how you get value from Fable. Instead, you give it context and let it plan. Fable's advantage is reasoning, not text generation. You set the goal and the constraints, Fable figures out how to get there, then Sonnet executes the steps. One high-quality Fable turn at the start of a session is worth more than five expensive Fable turns doing routine work.

Where Fable genuinely earns its cost. Interactive charts that need real logic behind them, not just visual formatting. Spreadsheets with complex dependencies — twelve tabs, real formulas, board-ready. Deep market research across hundreds of sources where the synthesis has to be accurate, not just plausible. Co-writing anything where you've uploaded everything about yourself and need the output to actually sound like you. Deck generation where the argument structure matters. The pattern: tasks where being wrong is costly, or where the output will be seen by people who can tell.

beats.narration_text: Where Fable is pure waste. Summarizing a document you already understand. Reformatting something. Drafting a routine email. Generating three LinkedIn caption options. Answering a factual question with a known answer. These are Sonnet tasks — or even Haiku tasks. The failure mode is psychological: people reach for the smartest model because it feels safer. But Fable doesn't make simple tasks better. It makes them expensive. The discomfort of using a cheaper model on a simple task is almost always wrong intuition.

The real danger is rollout without training. The rollout scenario: you give your team of a hundred people access to Fable-5 with no guidance on which model to use. They default to the smartest-sounding option — that's human behavior. Nobody tracks it because they don't know there's anything to track. Usage billing means the invoice grows silently. This is not a hypothetical. It's what happens in most enterprise AI rollouts. The fix is cheap: before you give anyone Fable access, write a one-paragraph decision rule. When to use Fable. When to use Sonnet. Post it somewhere everyone sees it.

props.title: team-model-rule.md
props.code:
# Model decision rule — post this for your team Use Fable-5 when:
- The task requires multi-step reasoning or strategy
- Being wrong would cost time, money, or credibility
- You are planning something a cheaper model will execute Use Sonnet-5 for everything else:
- Drafts, summaries, formatting, routine email
- Any task where a near-miss is acceptable When in doubt: start with Sonnet.
If the output is wrong, escalate to Fable.

beats.narration_text: The important limit is what Fable-5 doesn't fix. It doesn't fix a bad brief. If you give it vague instructions, it produces a confident-sounding, well-structured version of vague. It doesn't fix missing context — if you don't tell it what your company does, it guesses. And it doesn't fix the habit of not reviewing outputs. Fable makes fewer mistakes than Sonnet. It does not make zero mistakes. The senior lawyer still needs a client who reads the contract.
